desc:
Imagine the tree drawn on a complete binary tree frame: the root has slot 1, and a node in slot p has its left child in slot 2p and its right child in slot 2p + 1. The width of a level is (slot of its rightmost node) - (slot of its leftmost node) + 1, so missing nodes between the two ends count too. Return the largest width over all levels. The empty tree has width 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 3, 2, 5, 3, -1, 9] the last level has nodes in slots 4, 5 and 7, so its width is 7 - 4 + 1 = 4.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
The tree has at most 30 levels, so every width fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Only the leftmost and the rightmost node of every level matter for the width of that level.
Give every node a slot number: 2p for a left child and 2p + 1 for a right child. Slots on the same level are comparable, so the width is the largest minus the smallest slot plus one.
Process nodes in level order and keep the minimum and maximum slot per level. In Python integers are unbounded; in other languages subtract the first slot of the level to keep numbers small.
editorial: Slot numbering turns the picture of the complete binary tree into arithmetic. On any level the slots of different nodes are different, and the order of slots equals the left-to-right order, so the first node met on a level has the smallest slot and the last one the largest. The width of the level is their difference plus one.

Scan the nodes in level order, store the slot of every node, and keep for each level its first and last slot. The answer is the maximum of last - first + 1. Slots grow like 2depth, which is why the number of levels is limited here; in a language with fixed-width integers subtract the first slot of the level before doubling (re-basing each level) to stay safe on deep trees.
